strengths: Well-motivated problem: streaming/sequential data settings are pervasive (sensor streams, databases), and the paper correctly identifies that existing TNP variants lack cheap incremental updates, requiring full context re-encoding at quadratic cost per observation.

Clean and effective adaptation of causal masking and KV caching to Transformer Neural Processes. The method is clearly described (Eqs. 3-4, Eqs. 13-16, Figure 7), and the computational analysis in Appendix F rigorously derives the O(N) vs O(N²) per-step and O(N²) vs O(N³) cumulative cost reductions, matching the empirical runtime curves (Figures 5, 17).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning synthetic 1D GP regression, synthetic tabular data, four real-world UCI regression datasets (Skillcraft, Powerplant, Elevators, Protein), and HadISD temperature prediction, evaluated in both factorised and autoregressive deployment modes.

The dense autoregressive training strategy (incTNP-Seq) is a genuinely useful contribution: it amortises learning across all prefix context sizes in a single forward pass and empirically yields lower variance across hyperparameter configurations (Figure 2, Figure 11), which is convincingly demonstrated via learning-rate/schedule sweeps.

The implicit Bayesianness analysis (Section 4.4, 5.2, Proposition 4.1, Appendix C) is a novel and thoughtful application of the KL-gap metric to NPs, and the finding that incTNP retains a KL gap comparable to permutation-invariant TNP-D (Figures 3, 13) is an interesting, non-trivial result that strengthens the streaming argument.

Good robustness and fairness practices: compute-matched baselines (stars in Figure 2), standard errors reported in Table 2, out-of-distribution 24-hour window evaluation (Table 3), and a distribution-shift study (Appendix G).
Reproducibility is well supported: code provided, detailed optimiser/architecture/hyperparameter specifications in Appendix B, and hardware details in Appendix A.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: causal masking and KV caching are standard, well-established LLM techniques, and their adaptation to TNPs is fairly direct once stated. The paper reads more as a careful engineering transfer than a new algorithmic idea.

The central empirical claim—that causal masking does not degrade predictive performance—is repeatedly labelled 'surprising' but is never mechanistically explained. Why causal masking is benign for set-valued NP prediction (versus LLMs) is not investigated, which is a missed opportunity to provide genuine new understanding.

Several results are marginal or within noise: on 1D GP, incTNP-Seq differs from TNP-D by only -0.002 (±0.0019 SEM); on Elevators, incTNP is -0.024 and incTNP-Seq is -0.009. The claim of 'matching or outperforming' thus rests on very small differences in multiple settings.

The factorised temperature-forecasting result (+0.690 for incTNP-Seq, Table 1a) is anomalously large relative to interpolation (+0.018) and is not explained or interrogated; such a gap warrants scrutiny (e.g., whether it reflects a prior-mismatch artefact rather than a genuine modelling advantage).

The implicit Bayesianness metric is adapted from Mlodozeniec et al. (2024) rather than newly developed, and the empirical Bayesianness study is limited to 1D GP data with small context sizes (20 or 3 fixed context points, 40 or 100 targets), leaving the generalisation of this finding to the tabular/temperature domains untested.

Overlap with Hassan et al. (2025) is significant—they also target efficient autoregressive inference for transformer probabilistic models. The distinction (streaming vs. correlated-target generation, no buffer) is argued in Section 3.2/E.2, but the conceptual boundary is narrower than the paper implies.

KV-cache memory growth is acknowledged only briefly in the conclusion and never quantified; for the claimed 30,000-point streams this could be a practical bottleneck that is not empirically characterized.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: efficient incremental updates for Transformer Neural Processes in streaming settings, where existing TNPs suffer from quadratic recomputation costs.
Simple and effective adaptation of causal masking and KV caching from LLMs to TNPs, enabling O(N) context updates and supporting both factorised and autoregressive streaming inference.

The dense autoregressive training strategy (incTNP-Seq) is a useful contribution: it amortises learning across all prefix context sizes in a single forward pass and empirically improves performance and hyperparameter robustness.

Extensive experiments across synthetic 1D GP regression, synthetic and real-world tabular regression (UCI datasets), and a real-world temperature prediction task (HadISD), including factorised and AR deployment modes.
Clear theoretical complexity analysis and empirical runtime comparisons showing linear versus quadratic per-update scaling, with additional cumulative cost analysis in the appendix.
Introduces the implicit Bayesianness metric to the NP literature, including a proof of the KL-gap decomposition and comparison against a streaming GP baseline (WISKI).
Reproducibility is generally well-supported: detailed appendix with data generation, hyperparameters, hardware, training procedures, and code provided in the supplementary material.
Honest limitations discussion in the conclusion, covering distribution shift, active learning, extreme context scaling, KV-cache memory, and possible SSM backbones.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: causal masking and KV caching are standard techniques in LLMs, and applying them to TNPs is a relatively straightforward adaptation. The dense autoregressive training is also closely related to standard autoregressive training.

Overstated claims: the abstract and introduction claim 'orders-of-magnitude speedups', but the presented experiments show at most ~3.5x speedup in AR mode and ~5x in streaming cumulative cost; orders-of-magnitude gains are only asymptotic and not demonstrated at the tested scales.

Conceptual flaw in the implicit Bayesianness analysis: the metric measures exchangeability, but streaming data are generally not exchangeable. Proposition 4.1 assumes an exchangeable true data-generating distribution, yet the paper generalises conclusions to streaming settings. The metric is only evaluated on 1D GP regression (exchangeable data), so the claim that incTNP is 'no less Bayesian' in streaming is not supported for non-exchangeable tasks such as temperature forecasting.

The KL-gap estimation approximates an average over 40! permutations using only 256 permutations and 32 Monte Carlo samples for the KL divergence. No convergence or bias/variance analysis is provided, so the reliability of the implicit Bayesianness results is questionable.

The comparison to TNP-D conflates architecture and training strategy. incTNP-Seq uses a different training objective that provides dense supervision over all prefixes; TNP-D cannot use this objective. Although compute-equal training is attempted, the headline claim that 'incTNP matches TNP-D' is misleading because vanilla incTNP (causal masking without dense training) often underperforms TNP-D.

Performance gains are modest on many tasks (e.g., 0.002–0.036 nats improvement in log-likelihood). The large gain on temperature forecasting is on a transfer scenario where TNP-D itself performs worse than CNP, making the comparison less meaningful as a test of the method's general superiority.

The robustness claim based on Figure 2 involves 'filtering for outliers', but the filtering criteria are unspecified. This could artificially reduce variance and bias the conclusion that incTNP-Seq is more robust.
Reproducibility statement contains a blank URL ('available at') for the code, although the appendix says code is in the supplementary material. The missing link is a minor but avoidable omission.

Presentation issues: typos ('stategy'), inconsistent description of the implicit Bayesianness metric (the related work says 'proposing an alternative metric' while the main text says 'adapting' an existing metric), and confusing figure labels (e.g., Figure 5 right labels O(N^2) vs O(N) for per-update cost, while cumulative costs differ).

Missing comparison to closely related recent work by Hassan et al. (2025) on efficient autoregressive inference for transformer probabilistic models. The paper discusses it qualitatively but does not include it as an empirical baseline, despite its direct relevance.

The implicit Bayesianness experiment is limited to a single synthetic 1D GP task with Nc=20 and Nt=40. It is unclear whether the conclusions generalise to higher-dimensional or real-world streaming tasks.
No empirical analysis of KV-cache memory complexity, even though this is a practical bottleneck for long streams; it is only mentioned as future work.

strengths: Addresses an important practical limitation of Transformer Neural Processes for streaming data: lack of cheap incremental updates. The motivation is clear and well-positioned relative to NPs, PFNs, and streaming GPs.

Introduces a simple and effective adaptation of causal masking and KV caching to TNPs, reducing per-update complexity from O(N^2) to O(N) and cumulative streaming cost from O(N^3) to O(N^2). The theoretical analysis is clear and supported by runtime measurements.

Proposes a dense autoregressive training strategy (incTNP-Seq) that amortizes learning across all context sizes, improving performance and hyperparameter robustness. Compute-equal comparisons in the appendix strengthen this claim.

Extensive empirical evaluation across synthetic GP regression, synthetic tabular data, four UCI datasets, and a real-world temperature prediction task (HadISD), in both factorised and autoregressive modes, with appropriate baselines (TNP-D, CNP, LBANP, WISKI, TNP-A) and reported standard errors.

Adapts and applies an implicit Bayesianness metric to NPs, providing a quantitative analysis of how causal masking affects predictive consistency. The result that incTNP-Seq has a KL gap comparable to TNP-D is interesting and practically relevant.
Reproducibility is supported by a detailed appendix (data generation, hyperparameters, hardware), and the implementation is stated to be available.
weaknesses: There is a train-test mismatch for incTNP-Seq: during training it uses masked cross-attention so that each target token attends only to preceding context/target tokens, but at inference it uses unmasked cross-attention to the full context set (and in factorised mode does not attend to other targets). This undermines the claim that incTNP-Seq is a principled drop-in replacement for TNP-D in both factorised and autoregressive modes; the strong factorised results are not fully explained by the training objective.

The core technical novelty is limited: causal masking and KV caching are standard techniques from LLMs, and applying them to TNPs is a straightforward engineering adaptation. The dense autoregressive training is also directly inspired by LLM training. The theoretical decomposition in Proposition 4.1 is a known result.

The implicit Bayesianness analysis is only performed on 1D GP regression. The conclusion that incTNP retains consistency comparable to TNP-D may not generalize to higher-dimensional tabular or spatiotemporal tasks, where the metric is not evaluated.

For static context settings, incTNP is not permutation invariant with respect to the context set. The paper does not quantify how sensitive its predictions are to context ordering in static tasks, where the order is arbitrary. This could affect the claimed parity with TNP-D.

Some claims are overstated. The abstract advertises 'orders-of-magnitude speedups', but the static AR table shows only ~3.5x on the temperature task; the order-of-magnitude gain appears only for long streams. The claim of matching or exceeding TNP-D is not universally true (e.g., 1D GP and Elevators are slightly worse, albeit within SEM).
The main text does not discuss the train-test mismatch or the order-sensitivity limitation, and the limitations section is relatively brief, focusing on memory and distribution shift.

strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck: streaming NP inference requires recomputing context representations, and incTNP uses causal masking plus KV caching to reduce per-update conditioning from O(Ns^2) to O(Ns), with detailed per-step and cumulative runtime/memory analyses in Appendices F-G.

The dense autoregressive training strategy (incTNP-Seq) is a useful adaptation: it provides supervision for all prefix contexts in one forward pass, improves data efficiency, and empirically stabilizes hyperparameter sensitivity (Fig. 2, Appendix E.1.3).

Broad empirical evaluation: synthetic GP, synthetic tabular, four real UCI tabular datasets, and HadISD temperature interpolation/forecasting, in both factorised and AR modes, with comparisons to TNP-D, CNP, LBANP, TNP-A, and WISKI.

The implicit Bayesianness analysis adapts an exchangeability/KL-gap framework to NPs, provides proofs (Propositions 4.1 and 4.2), and offers an empirical protocol; the finding that incTNP-Seq's KL gap is comparable to TNP-D on 1D GP is interesting and well-motivated.
Reproducibility details are strong: code in the supplement, hardware specifications, optimiser settings, data-generation protocols, hyperparameters, and training procedures are documented.
Limitations are candidly discussed: loss of permutation invariance, KV-cache memory costs, incTNP-Seq training cost, and future directions such as state-space models.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: causal masking and KV caching are standard transformer techniques, and the dense prefix/AR training objective is closely related to causal language modelling. The core contribution is an application/adaptation rather than a new architectural principle.

Main experimental comparisons use a single training seed per model (Appendix B), so reported standard errors reflect test-task variation rather than training variability. Claims of parity or outperformance, especially for small differences, are not robustly established across seeds.

Performance is not uniformly matched: e.g., factorised Elevators incTNP-Seq is -0.0086 relative to TNP-D with SEM around 0.0004, a clear loss, and 1D GP factorised is slightly worse. The abstract claim of matching or exceeding TNP-D is therefore somewhat overstated.

Compute-matching is not fully consistent across all experiments. incTNP-Seq has higher per-step training cost O((Nc+Nt)^2); while compute-equal baselines are reported for some GP/tabular robustness experiments, the main tables and temperature experiments appear to use fixed epochs rather than fully equal compute, weakening the 'equal training budget' claim.

Implicit Bayesianness evidence is narrow: it is evaluated only on 1D GP regression under a teacher-forced one-at-a-time protocol, with no real-data or AR-deployment validation. The conclusion that incTNP is 'no less Bayesian' than TNP-D is therefore specific rather than general.

No empirical comparison is provided to the most closely related recent work, Hassan et al. (2025), which also targets efficient autoregressive NP inference; a direct comparison would clarify practical advantages.

The paper sacrifices context permutation invariance, and although Appendix H analyzes sensitivity, the main paper does not fully quantify how this affects downstream reliability/calibration, especially for non-stationary or adversarially ordered streams.

Presentation is dense and occasionally imprecise: notation around incTNP-Seq's target stream indexing/masking is confusing (Appendix B, Eq. 18-19), and there are minor typos/overstatements such as 'computer-matched budget'.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: efficient incremental updates for Transformer Neural Processes in streaming settings. The proposed solution—adapting causal masking and KV caching from LLMs—is straightforward but effective.

The computational complexity analysis (Section 4.3, Appendices F and G) is thorough, covering both factorised and autoregressive modes, and is supported by empirical runtime measurements showing the expected quadratic-to-linear improvement in update cost.

The dense autoregressive training strategy (incTNP-Seq) is a clever adaptation that amortises training across all context sizes and appears to improve both performance and robustness, as evidenced by the hyperparameter sensitivity analysis in Figure 2.

The empirical evaluation is broad, spanning synthetic GP regression, tabular data (synthetic and UCI benchmarks), and a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction task, with comparisons to strong baselines (TNP-D, TNP-A, CNP, LBANP, WISKI).

The adaptation of the implicit Bayesianness metric to NPs is a novel and interesting contribution. The theoretical decomposition (Propositions 4.1 and 4.2) is correct, and the empirical results (Figure 3) provide useful insight into the consistency of incTNP compared to TNP-D.

The paper is generally well-written and clear, with good visualisations (e.g., Figure 1 for complexity, Figure 3 for implicit Bayesianness) and a comprehensive appendix that provides detailed experimental setups and additional results.
weaknesses: The core idea—applying causal masking and KV caching to enable incremental updates—is not methodologically novel; it is a direct adaptation of well-known techniques from the LLM literature. The contribution is thus primarily engineering-focused rather than introducing a fundamentally new concept.

The theoretical analysis of implicit Bayesianness (Section 4.4) does not provide new theoretical guarantees for incTNP specifically; it adapts existing results and shows that non-exchangeability leads to a KL gap, but does not prove that incTNP's order sensitivity is small. The claim that incTNP is 'practically no less Bayesian' relies solely on empirical evidence, which, while suggestive, is limited to specific tasks and configurations.

The empirical results, although broad, are not always conclusive. For instance, in Table 1(a), incTNP-Seq underperforms TNP-D on the 1D GP task and Elevators dataset. While the paper notes these are within one SEM or due to underfitting, it weakens the claim of consistent parity or superiority.

The dense autoregressive training strategy (incTNP-Seq) is computationally more expensive per step (O((N_c+N_t)^2) vs O(N_c^2 + N_c N_t)). The paper argues this is offset by better data efficiency, but the compute-matched comparison (Figure 2) shows that incTNP-Seq still outperforms, yet the margin is not overwhelming, and the analysis is limited to two datasets.

The paper does not isolate the effect of the training strategy from the architectural changes. It would be valuable to see incTNP trained with the standard meta-learning objective to disentangle the benefits of causal masking from those of dense autoregressive training.

The loss of permutation invariance is acknowledged, but its practical implications are not fully explored. The context ordering algorithm (Appendix H.3) and aggregation over permutations (Appendix H.4) are promising but relegated to the appendix and not integrated into the main experiments. The main text only briefly mentions this trade-off.

The experimental evaluation in the main text often reports relative differences (Δ) without absolute values for the proposed methods, making it harder to assess their standalone performance. The standard errors are provided in the appendix, but the main tables could be more informative.

The choice of random ordering for tabular data (Section B.2) is a potential weakness, as it may not reflect realistic streaming scenarios where data arrive in a meaningful order. The paper does not discuss the impact of ordering on performance in these tasks.

The efficiency gains are demonstrated primarily in terms of runtime, but the memory overhead of KV caching (O(L D_z N_s)) is a potential bottleneck for very long streams. The paper acknowledges this and suggests future work on cache eviction or SSMs, but does not provide a solution.

The paper claims 'orders-of-magnitude speedups' but the reported speedups in Table 1(b) are up to 3.57× for AR mode on temperature prediction. While significant, this is not orders of magnitude in the tested regimes; the cubic vs quadratic cumulative scaling would yield larger gains at much longer stream lengths, but those are not empirically demonstrated in the main text.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: existing TNP variants lack cheap incremental context updates, and the paper convincingly motivates the streaming setting (sensor streams, database updates, real-time weather) where this matters.

The core mechanism—causal masking plus KV caching adapted from LLMs to the TNP encoder, together with masked cross-attention—is simple, principled, and clearly effective. The complexity analysis (Appendix F) and memory analysis (Appendix G) are careful, distinguishing per-update O(Ns) vs O(Ns²) costs and cumulative O(Ns²) vs O(Ns³), and are supported by measured runtime and memory curves (Figs. 5, 14, 20, 21).

The dense autoregressive training strategy (incTNP-Seq) is a genuine methodological contribution: training on all prefix contexts in a single forward pass both amortizes supervision and empirically improves accuracy and hyperparameter robustness (Figs. 2, 10-13), with a plausible gradient-noise-to-signal-ratio analysis to support the robustness claim.

The adaptation of the implicit Bayesianness/KL-gap framework to the regression/streaming setting (Propositions 4.1-4.2, proofs in Appendix C) is a novel and thoughtful way to quantify the cost of sacrificing context permutation invariance, and the empirical finding that incTNP-Seq is roughly as Bayesian as TNP-D while outperforming approximate-GP baselines (WISKI) is interesting.

Empirical breadth is good: synthetic 1D GP (multiple kernels and context sizes), synthetic and four real UCI tabular tasks (including sim-to-real), and a real spatiotemporal HadISD temperature task in both interpolation and forecasting regimes, evaluated in static, streaming, factorised, and AR modes with SEMs reported.
Reproducibility is well-supported: code is provided, architectures and optimizers are specified in detail, and appendices cover hardware, data generation, and training protocols.

Limitations are treated honestly: the loss of context permutation invariance, KV-cache memory bottlenecks, single-seed results, and the teacher-forced nature of the Bayesianness protocol are all explicitly discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Novelty of the central mechanism is moderate. Causal masking + KV caching is standard in LLMs and has been applied to autoregressive NP inference before (e.g., Hassan et al. 2025, which the paper cites). The incremental contribution is the uniform application across the whole stream and the training strategy, but the architectural idea itself is not deeply new.

Results are from a single training seed per model ('Unless otherwise specified, all reported results are from a single training run... using a single training seed'), which limits confidence in the reported deltas, several of which are very small (e.g., Skillcraft +0.008, Powerplant +0.003). Reporting SEMs across test datasets does not substitute for seed-level variance.

The 'orders-of-magnitude' speedup claim is somewhat overstated relative to what is shown; measured speedups are ~3.5x at Ns=100k, with the asymptotic advantage only becoming dramatic at very large streams. The headline framing outpaces the presented evidence in the mid-range regime.

The implicit Bayesianness analysis is limited to 1D GP regression under a single teacher-forced, one-at-a-time protocol; the paper itself acknowledges alternative protocols (batched streaming, length generalisation, error compounding) are untested, so the generality of the 'no less Bayesian' conclusion is uncertain.

The factorised temperature-forecasting result for incTNP-Seq (+0.690) is anomalously large and is attributed to 'highly correlated targets and train-test mismatch' without a fully convincing mechanistic explanation; this deserves more scrutiny.
The comparison to the most directly related prior work (Hassan et al. 2025) is mostly qualitative; a head-to-head empirical comparison in the streaming setting would strengthen the positioning.

Some theoretical material (Propositions 4.1/4.2 and Appendix C) is largely an adaptation of Mlodozeniec et al. (2024) to the regression case; the incremental theoretical contribution is modest, though the empirical application to NPs is new.
